utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar please call the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today, on this Monday, I would like to first of all greet General Petkovic, who is our witness this week, and will be our witness over the following weeks. I would like to greet the accused as well, the Defence teams, Mr. Scott and all his colleagues and assistants, and I would also like to greet everyone else assisting us. First of all, I would like to provide you with a piece of information of an administrative nature that concerns April, the month of April. First of all, as I have already said, there will be no hearing on Monday, the 19th of April; on Tuesday, the 20th; on Wednesday, the 21st of April; and on Thursday, the 22nd of April. In addition, the Chamber has taken into account Mr. Karnavas' intervention last time, and we have also taken into account the comments that Mr. Scott made. And, therefore, the Chamber has also decided that on Tuesday, the 6th of April, and Wednesday, the 7th of April, no hearings will be held. So the 6th and 7th of April. And this means that the Coric Defence should schedule its witness in accordance with these decisions. They should take these dates into account when compiling their schedule. We will resume on the 8th of April, for example, and on the 8th of April you could call a witness, who will witness on that day. It's for you to see. I know this is an extremely complicated exercise, calling witnesses is a complicated exercise, but it's best to be aware of these facts in advance. That's what I wanted to inform you of. General Petkovic, I am now going to continue putting my questions to you. Last week, I said that I would deal with the issue of a criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Petkovic. Is there something you wanted to say? You raised your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour Antonetti. With your leave, I'd like a minute to add certain things to what I said the previous day. I think it's very important. So with your leave, before you continue, I'd like to add a few things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, this has to do with the subject of my testimony on the first two cases. I would like to inform you of the fact that as a witness of the Chamber, it was my duty to fill in a form, state the conditions, and provide the Chamber with information. The Chamber would answer the request and say they accept this, and then they would set a date for my testimony. That's all I wanted to say. In one case, in accordance with the law and the Court's regulations, I personally had to inform the Chamber of certain things. I did that in both cases, and I think that these documents form part of the archives. That's all I wanted to do say. We can now proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to what we said last week, there are two follow-up questions I would like to put to you before I deal with the issue of joint criminal enterprise. Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, General Petkovic, I would like to know whether at any point in time --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have translation, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start again. General Petkovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's strange, because whenever I want to put an important question, we have an interpretation problem. It's quite extraordinary. So listen to my question carefully. I would like to know, General Petkovic, before the indictment was drawn up by this Tribunal, had you been interviewed by the OTP or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no one interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that when you came to testify in the Blaskic case, no one had put questions of any kind to you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which questions you have in mind. The questions put by the Chamber, the Prosecution, and the Defence, and afterwards no other questions were put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I wanted to say is that before you came to testify in the Blaskic case, the OTP hadn't established contact with you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, they hadn't established contact with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Over the weekend, I thought about putting the following question to you. We know that you were a member of three armies, the JNA, the Croatian Army, and the HVO. We know that for sure. And perhaps you were also a member of the ABiH army, but we'll see about that in the judgement. What I'd like to know, as you were a member of these various armies, did you find any differences between these various armies? And if so, what kind of differences? For example, I was in a certain functioning within a legal system of a certain kind. When I came here, I noted that there were certain differences. In my system, for example, I had the impression that we were a lot more rigorous. And, secondly, in my system the other judges don't put questions. It's only the presiding judge who puts questions. So those are two main differences. When I came here, I noted that the system was different. So what I would like to know is whether you, yourself, when you moved from the JNA and joined the Croatian Army and then the HVO, did you notice any differences? And if so, what kind of differences?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, there were differences. The JNA was an institution that had been formed throughout the war. It established a structure of its own. It had a certain continuity. It had its officers, non-commissioned officers. It had a system for operative deployment which had been developed. That was for the entire JNA. There was a system of territorial defence, and everyone else included in this, and in a certain system one knew exactly who the commander was of the 1st Detachment, for example, of the 3rd Company, of the 1st Battalion in a certain partisan brigade. He knew it, his family knew it, and so on and so forth. So it was a very organised system that had been developed. For many years, people knew each other, and it had a basis of its own. I'd also like to add, however, that when the war broke out in that area and when that system -- when that structure started losing certain members, Slovenians, Croats, and later Muslims, Bosniaks, it had certain organisational problems and problems of different kinds. When a certain structure or system starts losing a certain number of members, it's hard to bring it back up to strength. But, nevertheless, it was a system from the lowest unit up until a state which was completely integrated; it had its developed plans, plans that had been fully developed. Whereas, on the other hand, the Croatian Army couldn't structure itself while Croatia was part of the JNA. It didn't lose its territorial defence. Croatia had its own territorial defence, and that was strongest and best-equipped territorial defences in the former republics. However, that system was a system it lost in its entirety. Not a single brigade, as far as I know, or reserve brigade or territorial brigade from that time, not a single such brigade remained as a whole within the Croatian Army, as part of the Croatian Army. All of them, with some of the men and with all the equipment, were moved to the JNA side. And that's what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina, too, when the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was dismantled, so to speak. So the Croatian Army, and later the HVO and then the BiH -- well, combat had already started. The JNA had already taken its positions, and they had to gather men, organise themselves, although they had no developed commands or staffs. They had to decide who would command whom, and when. So one went to war without having any sort of a system. One went to war against an army that had developed its structure over many years. So the differences were enormous. In the JNA, you knew that if a brigade consists of 2.500 men, then it will be there throughout the war. Perhaps it will be brought up to strength, 30 per cent will be reinforced. But in the HVO, the Croatian Army and the ABiH knew their system of working was brought in. To maintain a brigade of 3.000 -- or 2.000 men, you had to mobilise 10.000 men over a three-month period, because had you to take into account the social dimension, you had to take into account the fact that people couldn't be separated from their families for a very long time. They had to remain in contact with their way the life, so such were the conditions. The differences were great; you can't compare the JNA, which was an organised army at the time, with the armies that were being formed. The Croatian Army became developed in front -- just before the Operations Storm and the other operation. The Croatian Army had a stage when, in 1992, UNPROFOR came, and also the forces were minimal at the time at the UNPROFOR lines, the lines separated by UNPROFOR, and the other forces could train. And that's how the Croatian Guards Brigades were formed, and later they demonstrated that they were stronger than the JNA brigades and the brigades of the Army of Republika Srpska or the brigades of the Bosnian Serbs. The HVO and the ABiH didn't have a single day to rest in order to gather formed units and work with them and train them, so that was the difference. It was a significant difference, if you're familiar with military structure. So the Croatian Army started to develop before the two operations, Flash and Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I'd like to correct the transcript. Page 7, line 3, it says that the general said that the Croatian Army became a developed army just before the Operations Flash and Storm. It hasn't been correctly transcribed. I think it's important, because it was in 1995. So we want to know which operations he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that answer, which will help us to take into account these differences. One last question before I deal with the joint criminal enterprise issue. Last week, you provided us with details of the dates when you were in Geneva to attend the conference. Apparently you went there three times. I don't have the transcript before me, however. I would like to know where the conference was being held. Was it in a hotel, or was it in the International Geneva Conference Centre, or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was in the facilities of the International -- well, I don't know if these facilities are UN facilities. It was in the centre, as you called it. It was a fairly large complex a few minutes from Hotel International or Inter-Continental, whatever it is. I thought it was a complex that belonged to the UN or something like that. So that's where the conference was held. It wasn't held in a hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Were all the delegations staying in the same hotel, or did they stay in different hotels?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. It depended on the reservations one managed to make. I was in the Hotel International on the first occasion and then I spent time in some other mid-range hotels in the vicinity. Well, you know, in Geneva it's always quite crowded in the hotels, so on one occasion you'd be in one hotel, on another occasion in another hotel, but the delegations weren't always in the same place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The delegation led by Mate Boban, was that delegation in a hotel on its own, or were you there together with a delegation from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first time when I went there, I was in that hotel. I think we were on the 13th floor; myself, Mr. Boban, Bila Mandzic, and two others who accompanied Mate Boban. On the second occasion, I was there, Mr. Mandzic and another professor from Sarajevo. There was no place there, and it was also expensive, you know, so I don't really remember the name, but there was a small hotel perhaps 15 minutes away from the hotel we had previously stayed in, on foot, that's where we stayed. I don't know whether there's a hotel called Hotel President or something like that. Mr. Izetbegovic would sometimes be there. The Serbs were also there on one or two occasions -- or, rather, in the Hotel International. On the second occasion, I don't know where they stayed. And if we stayed in Hotel International, then there were two or three floors that separated the delegations, and there was security that was present. They were in civilian clothing. There was security for each delegation present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now for my last question. When you would meet with the delegations, was there a little flag on the desk, or no flag, just the names saying "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," "Croatian Defence Council," and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, these were plenary sessions. The only information provided concerned the identity of the people sitting at certain places. There was the delegation from Yugoslavia at the first table. Then there was the delegation from Croatia. And then we, from the HVO, were there. Next to me there was Mr. Izetbegovic's delegation. So we were sitting in a circular fashion. Representatives were in front of us, and no one had flags or signs of any kind in front of them. I think that all we had were names in front of each individual. Sometimes we would go to the chairman's office. He would call the delegation to talk about constitutional principles or maps. The discussion would last for an hour or two, and then a second delegation would go there, and during that time others would remain in some other office, a small office. That's where they would wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I'm putting a very technical question to you. I, myself, participated in such international conferences, and I know how things can proceed. I'll conclude with a minor technical detail. Did you have a badge on you that allowed you freedom of movement, or were there no badges for anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we didn't have any badges, signs of any kind, but we were told in which areas we could move around in. As far as I can remember, the halls where plenary sessions were held and about ten officers were concerned, there was a large hall and beyond those premises it wasn't possible to go, no one could go anywhere else. There were sandwiches, there were drinks that were provided. One could help oneself to these things. And we'd stay there until 4.00, 5.00, or 6.00 in the afternoon, but no one could go out and walk around in other areas of that complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the president of the conference addressed you, Mate Boban, President Izetbegovic, Karadzic - I assume he was there too - what would he say? Would he say, Mr. Boban, or would he also add the title of the person he was addressing and his function?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I can remember, as far as I can remember, it was just "Mr.," and the name of the person he was addressing. But I think President Tudjman, Cosic -- once, I think, President Cosic was there, too, Milosevic, and Izetbegovic, he would use the expression "Mr. President." But it depended. Mostly, he would say, Gentlemen, but there was no direct communication. It would be the first delegation would start speaking, and then the next, and after that we would have bilateral contacts. The military section went with General Nambiar to a special room and would continue the discussion there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Petkovic, I'm now going to address the question of joint criminal enterprise appearing in paragraph 15 of the indictment. First of all, I wish to ask you, however, whether you had the totality of the indictment in your own language.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did you also have the pre-trial document in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed with the pre-trial brief, through the intermediary of my counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you know, as you must have read and re-read this document, you know this, and I will address the same -- I addressed it also to General Praljak, and you will know that the Prosecutor says that from or before the 18th of November, this word "before" is important, 1991 to about April 1994 and thereafter, again an important word, various persons in the [indiscernible] established a joint criminal enterprise and participated in it in order to politically and militarily subjugate the Bosnian Muslims and other known Croats who lived in areas on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were claimed to be part of the Croatian Community, and in brackets "(and later Republic of Herceg-Bosna)," and to permanently remove and to ethnically cleanse these areas, and to rally these in the short term or the long term, within a Greater Croatia, either by annexation to the Republic of Croatia or in close association with it, and to do so by force, fear, or threat of force, persecution, imprisonment, and detention, forcible transfer and deportation, appropriation and destruction of property, and other means which constituted or involved the commission of crimes which are punishable under Articles 2, 3, and 5 of the Tribunal's Statute. The joint criminal enterprise had, as its ambition, to establish a Croatian territory with the borders of the Croatian Banovina, a territorial entity that existed from 1939 to 1941. It was part of the joint criminal enterprise to engineer the political and ethnic map of these areas so that they would be Croat-dominated, both politically and demographically. That is what the Prosecutor says with respect to this joint criminal enterprise. What would be your reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My response, Your Honour, is that that is not true, and that it doesn't correspond to the truth, and that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina had no intention of subjugating anyone, to discriminate against anyone in any way. There was no intention on the part of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina to divide or cut up Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the contrary, the Croats started the war in the intention of preserving Bosnia and Herzegovina, as they supported it as an independent state. Therefore, I reject these statements in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The persons who, according to the Prosecutor, participated in this enterprise, I'm going to tell you their name, and then I'm going to ask you about each one of them. The persons are the following: Franjo Tudjman, president of the Republic of Croatia, who died on the 10th of December, 1999; Bosko [as interpreted] Susak, who died on the 3rd of May, 1998; Janko Bobetko, general of the Croatian Army, who died on the 29th of April, 2002; Mate Boban, president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, who died in July 1997. These are the people who are dead. Now the living: Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, Slobodan Praljak, yourself, Valentin Coric, Berislav Pusic, Dario Kordic, Tihomir Blaskic, and Mladen Naletilic. We're going to cover all of them to see whether you knew them. Mr. Tudjman, did you know him? And if so, when did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course I knew Mr. Tudjman, because I knew that he wanted the elections in the Republic of Croatia -- or, rather, when he started the election campaign, the first elections in the Republic of Croatia. I met President Tudjman for the first time in Geneva in January 1993, never before that date. President Tudjman never came to Dalmatia to visit the army there, for me to meet him there. My position in the Croatian Army was such that I didn't go to Zagreb, to the Main Headquarters, nor was I invited in any sense which would enable me to have contact with President Franjo Tudjman. Therefore, my first contact with President Tudjman, when I was close to him, was when we were called by the co-chairman, and this meeting happened on the 2nd of January, 1993, in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I am understanding you correctly, before the 2nd of January, 1993, you had no conversation with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, Your Honours. I didn't have any conversations with him. I didn't have occasion to meet President Tudjman and to be anywhere in his vicinity before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that before the 2nd of January, 1993, if President Tudjman had an idea of creating a Greater Croatia, he did not tell you about it before the 2nd of January, 1993, because you hadn't seen him before that date?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so. I hadn't seen him, I had no contact with him, nor did I read anywhere that President Tudjman had any such intentions, potential intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us move on to Mr. Gojko Susak. When did you meet him, and under which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, also in Geneva, on the 2nd of January, 1993, because Gojko Susak at the time was a member of the delegation of the Republic of Croatia. Before that, I didn't have occasion to meet Gojko Susak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the same question. Before the 2nd of January, 1993, so you were unable to discuss with Mr. Susak the Banovina, Greater Croatia, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to number 3, General Bobetko. When did you meet him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 10th of April, 1992, in Ploce, in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the 10th of April, 1992, what did he tell you on that date?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of April, 1992, I and General Bobetko discussed the situation after the JNA and the VRS had attacked HVO in the municipalities of Kupres, as a whole, a part of the municipality of Tomislavgrad, a part of the municipality of Livno, and the possible consequences of the defeat of the HVO regarding further developments in Herzegovina but also the southern part of the Republic of Croatia. And because of this situation which was developing especially in Kupres, General Bobetko travelled to the southern part of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you met General Bobetko in April 1992, did he discuss with you the issue of a Greater Croatia, the Banovina, the plan to redesign the ethnic map of this region so that the Croats would dominate? Did he speak to you about all this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. He made no mention of any such things. As I said, he mentioned developments in Western Herzegovina, the situation east of the Neretva, around the Neretva River, and how to liberate the part leading to the south of the Republic of Croatia in the direction of Dubrovnik. That was the only issue that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my understanding is that the meeting that you had with General Bobetko was focused exclusively on the defence of the Republic of Croatia, in view of the offensive by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so, Your Honour, that is what we discussed, and how to halt the Serb offensive -- or, rather, to launch a counter-offensive and liberate the south of the Republic of Croatia, because forces of the UN were not deployed there. So Croatia was allowed, if possible, to liberate the southern part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move on to Mate Boban. You already told us last week, but as the transcript would be read in its entirety, let me ask you the same question. Can you tell me, once again, when exactly you met Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was at the end of March 1992. It was in Metkovici, in the Narona Hotel, when I and my assistant for logistics were meant to sign a contract with this hotel on the preparation of food for the Croatian Army that was in the south of Croatia, and then a man approached me, and I was later told and introduced to him as Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did Mate Boban address you, talking to you, or was he just there and you didn't have any discussions between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, my assistant for logistics before the war was a commander of a large tourist settlement in the area of Split, and Mate Boban was the manager of a commercial enterprise in Imotski, which is the hinterland of Split, and they had very successful business relations throughout the period that Mr. Boban was the manager of this company, so they knew each other. And that was how he introduced me to Mr. Boban. That is how we met in that hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So your assistant for logistics, as you told us last week, introduced you to Mate Boban. And on that occasion is Mate Boban going to say to you, Look here, I want to re-establish the Banovina, I want a Greater Croatia, I want the Croats to be the majority, et cetera, et cetera? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. Mr. Boban asked me to tell him whether Neum was safe, because the Croatian Army had stopped the advance of the JNA just in front of Neum, and whether Metkovic and the Neretva River Valley were safe, and whether the Croatian Army could defend these areas. And I provided him with information to the effect that for several months now the Croatian Army was holding positions there and that the Serb forces had not managed to break through, and I said that we hoped that we would continue to do so. And then we talked about the situation in the Neretva River Valley, because it was normal that we depended on developments in the territory from Capljina to Mostar. And he told us what he knew about the forces which had already gained control over certain JNA facilities, and we already heard about that from General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mate Boban was the supreme commander of the HVO, and you were the chief of staff of the HV, the Croatian Army. So these two positions, his own and yours, were you led to meet, and how frequently, and were there any witnesses, or were you just tete-a-tete, just the two of you alone? There's an error in the transcript. I don't usually look at the transcript, but at the witness. But in line 25, you were the chief of staff of the HVO and not the HV. Very well. Could you answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me say first that Mate Boban was not the supreme commander at the time. These were just the beginnings of those local units in the territory of Herzegovina, and I was an operative officer in the headquarters of the Operative Zone of Split. Those were our respective positions. And I never spoke to Boban tete-a-tete. I think that our next meeting or conversation occurred either on the 1st of April or between the 1st and the 3rd of April, when he wanted to pass on that the JNA and the VRS were definitely launching an offensive in the area of Kupres, parts of Livno, and Tomislavgrad, and he asked me what the operative zone would do, because the area of Cim and everything south of Split would be at risk. So I simply told him that the operative zone would monitor the situation and that at this point in time the operative zone could not do anything more than that. But should combat operations start, we would see what the Main Staff of the Croatian Army would do. He then cautioned that it would be a good thing if the HVO were to be assisted in organisational terms, as it had no organisational structure yet, and that he really feared a forceful breakthrough from Western Herzegovina towards the Neretva River Valley and towards the Republic of Croatia. That was the conversation we had then. And I don't know whether on the 4th, when the attack started, whether he called the operative zone in Split to inform it about it, because at that point in time I was in the Neretva Valley. I was not in Split when the attack on Kupres started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So during this period of time until April 1992, you were in the Croatian Army's operative zone, but could you now tell me, very precisely, when exactly you had a meeting with Mate Boban, he as the supreme commander of the HVO, and you as the chief of staff of the HVO. When did this meeting -- this interview take place?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was a meeting on the 12th of April, 1992, at a point in time when the JNA managed to take control of the whole area; that is to say, of Western Herzegovina. And Mr. Boban arrived in Ploce to ask General Bobetko whether somebody was really going to assist the organisation of the defence to prevent Livno, Tomislavgrad, Prozor, and other places from falling, and I wasn't the chief of the Main Staff at the time. Now, the next meeting was on the 14th of April, that is to say, two days later, when I arrived in Grude. And there was a -- and I got to know Boban again for the third time, I met him again. And on the 15th of April, 1992, you saw the order from General Bobetko to set up a forward command post in Grude. And from that time on, I brought in -- on the 14th of April -- I was brought in on the 14th of April. I was only there three hours and returned to Ploce. But in official terms, the document was written on the 15th of April, 1992, when -- and you saw my appointment as head of the forward command post with several other people from the HVO. And from that time on, I spent time on the territory of Herzegovina or, rather, in the HVO on a continual basis, because a few days prior to that date the HVO was established, had been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if we have understood this correctly, in your opinion it's from the 15th of April, 1992, that you were the chief of staff of the HVO. At that point in time, was your immediate superior Mr. Mate Boban, from the military point of view?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but in 1992, not 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you say that it is correct. In military operations of a defensive or "offensive," in inverted commas, nature - I won't deal with the nuances now - in such operations everything you did as the chief of staff, was everything you did in that capacity strictly under the control of Mate Boban, the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mate Boban was the supreme commander, then nothing could be done without his knowledge, without him giving the okay. And they were defence operations towards Livno and Tomislavgrad to begin with, and then later on operations to liberate -- that is to say, in June 1992, to liberate the eastern bank of the Neretva River, and so on and so forth. And General Bobetko issued that part of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So as far as the Livno and Tomislavgrad areas are concerned, you say that at the time the orders were issued by General Bobetko, a general of the Croatian Army. But in your opinion, when exactly did Mate Boban don his supreme commander uniform, the uniform of the supreme commander of the HVO? When did he assume this role independently of the Croatian Army? Or perhaps he wasn't independent.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mate Boban took on that function for the first time on the 3rd of July, 1992, when the decree was passed governing the armed forces. Up until then, Mate Boban assigned himself as the president of the HVO and president of the HZ-HB, and not as the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you say that the key date is the 3rd of July, 1992. If I have understood you correctly, it is from that date onwards that Mate Boban assumed the role of the supreme commander of the military HVO. You have taken a solemn declaration. Please think about this carefully before answering. But could you tell me whether, from the 3rd of July, 1992, military operations conducted by the HVO, under your authority of the chief of staff of the HVO, could you tell me whether these operations were strictly controlled by Mate Boban, or were these operations under the control of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, I've already answered that and said that the first time the post of supreme commander was mentioned was in that decree. Up until that time, Mate Boban did pass certain acts, but he didn't sign, himself, as the supreme commander, because that was implied. As the president of the HZ-HB, he could pass certain acts, and it was understood that he was the person in command. But as a post, the post of supreme commander, the date mentioned is the 3rd of July, 1992. Now, in the border belt along the Neretva River Valley and towards Tomislavgrad, in those first three months, the orders were issued by General Bobetko. Mate Boban, and you saw this in some of the documents we looked at, dealt with other issues and other situations, but he was also politically involved in respect of these orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could you tell me, and it's very important, when, as far as you know, General Bobetko ceased issuing orders to troops in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was in September 1992. That was the definitive date. His last order was on the 13th of July, 1992, when he issued an order according to which parts of the Croatian Army which were located in the border belt should pull out towards the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Otherwise, the last meeting that he held was in September 1992, and then the entire command on the territory of the HVO -- well, the Main Staff of the HVO came to command the entire area and the whole of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we are making progress, because you were very precise there. You said that as of September 1992, General Bobetko ceased to issue orders. I will now deal with a very specific case to verify what you have just said. I'll take the situation in Prozor, Rama, as you wish, in October 1992. There were problems. I won't go into the details, because we spent hours discussing them. General Praljak explained to us that he went to the field to solve those problems. But you are testifying now, not General Praljak. When these events occurred, could you tell me whether at any point in time you, your subordinates, and even General Praljak, before doing anything else, before taking decisions of any other kind, did you pick up the phone, phone Zagreb, General Bobetko, Tudjman, Susak, in order to ask them what you should do; or were the Prozor events dealt with entirely by the HVO in a fully independent manner?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me first say this: General Bobetko at this point in time was dealing with the problem that he faced with the Yugoslav People's Army, which, on the basis of an agreement between Bobetko, Strugar and General Morillon, of the 15th of October, was supposed to pull out of the southern reaches of the Republic of Croatia east of Dubrovnik and to withdraw to the territory of Montenegro, which was the former Yugoslavia at the time. So General Bobetko in no way came into this area, least of all did anybody call Franjo Tudjman up, or Gojko Susak. And I think it was three days before that that I already started to prepare the operation in the Neretva River Valley against the Serbs which, from the Republic of Croatia, were engaged in withdrawing from that territory. And on the 18th, I think it was, I had already started to take up resources from the Operative Zone of South-West Herzegovina and transfer them to the Neretva River Valley. Three Howitzers of 122 millimetres, that's what I took. Yes, three Howitzers of 122 millimetres. And I think that was on the 17th or 18th of October. And I transferred them from that operative zone, that is to say, North-West Herzegovina, to the Neretva River Valley, with all the crews, with the ammunition, and all the other equipment. So at that point in time, all of us were engaged in preparing the operation in the Neretva River Valley, and that because the JNA forces and the Serb volunteer forces from the south of Croatia were pulling out, they were withdrawing to Eastern Herzegovina, and their attempt was that if they had lost the coast, they could return to the Neretva River Valley. So we were all geared towards this part and focused on the Neretva River Valley. So nobody at that point in time gave any thought to Prozor or any events -- or thought that anybody would be happening in Prozor. The only thing we did think about was Jajce, which, to all intents and purposes, had all but fallen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that in October, the HVO's concern and the concern of the Croatian Army was the Neretva Valley, they were concerned with the Neretva Valley, where there was a Serb presence, so we should, therefore, conclude that the Croatian Army wasn't concerned at that point in time with the HVO-ABiH issue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour. Just one correction. The Croatian Army at that time was not in the Neretva Valley. The Croatian Army was at the border between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, from Popovo Polje, and that's the place where Vojislav Seselj was born, stretching towards the border with Montenegro. Now, the HVO was now in control of the territory east of the River Neretva, Stolac municipality; not the whole of it, but 80 per cent of it, Eastern Mostar, Bijelo Polje, and so on, and was preparing for the operation I mentioned because of the concentration of Serb forces which, when they were pulling out of Croatia, instead of going to Montenegro, were coming in to the Trebinje-Nevesinje area and these municipalities to go back to the Neretva River. That was their goal. So they were defeated in Southern Croatia, but they wanted to seek satisfaction by going back to the Neretva River Valley. So the HVO had to start preparations for such an attack, and that was done at the beginning of November; 1992, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Petkovic, I'm putting these questions to you because in a certain manner I'm handicapped. I don't have at my disposal all the military documents from the Croatian Army. Similarly, I don't have at my disposal all the HVO military documents, and I don't have all the Serbian forces' documents at my disposal either. If I had all these documents at my disposal, I would place them before me, and I would compare these documents and try to determine whether, in Prozor-Rama, there was contact between the HVO and the Croatian Army, because there may have been orders, summaries, telephone intercepts. The Serbs may have certainly intercepted certain calls, and the truth would have come out. But as I don't have these documents, I'm putting these questions to you in this blind manner, and you are answering them under oath. So if I have understood matters correctly, in October 1992, when the Prozor events transpired, the Croatian Army, according to what you have said, was not at all concerned, not at all involved. So you have said this to me under oath. Perhaps the Prosecution will produce a telephone intercept or a document from his hat. I don't know. But you are saying that in October 1992, Serbs were one's main preoccupation, not the tensions between the HVO and the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, the Serbs were the Republic of Croatian's main preoccupation in October 1992, because Dubrovnik had been de-blocked, the south of Croatia had been liberated, and all that had to be done was to wait for the Yugoslav Army and parts of the Serb forces to pull out of the territory of the Republic of Croatia. And then along the border -- along the border belt, that the UN observers should take up their positions. So that was the time and area when General Bobetko and the Croatian Army -- where the Croatian Army did not have any other possibility. It sent all its forces to Dubrovnik to liberate the south of the Republic of Croatia finally, and it managed to do so in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I'm not going to insist on the Prozor municipality, but to remind everyone of the following. The events in Prozor are mentioned in paragraph 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, and in the following paragraphs, but mainly in those paragraphs. But I will read to you paragraph 49, and you will answer the question I will then put to you. Listen to me carefully: "On the evening of the 24th of October, 1992, an area HVO commander reported that Prozor town was 'ethnically pure,' the Muslim population having been detained or having fled." And listen to what follows carefully: "On the 26th of October, 1992, Bruno Stojic, Milivoj Petkovic, Janko Bobetko and others were informed that the HVO had taken control of Prozor on the 25th of October, with many casualties on the Muslim side." So the Prosecution is stating very clearly that Mr. Bobetko was familiar with these facts. What do you say about that? He was familiar because he was informed of them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I don't know where this man gets the right, who did not command anything in Prozor, to write something like that, to write a report like that to Janko Bobetko. So let's see what rank that person held, this Mr. Schmidt in Prozor. And he enumerates what he does and sends out this information to Janko Bobetko. Why he did that, I really don't know. But I maintain that Janko Bobetko has nothing to do with Prozor. Now, why this person mentions him in this regard, I'm really not quite clear on that. And I don't know where they sent this report. I don't have the document in front of me, but I have seen it. And I can also say that if you compare two documents, where it says "ethnically pure," "ethnically cleansed," it was somebody who did not know Croatian properly and copied it out from a document. I think it was from a document of the Rama Brigade, and it doesn't say "ethnically cleansed," it says something quite different there. And perhaps we can compare the two documents in due course and see. Anyway, this person had absolutely no reason for that -- to contact General Bobetko. General Bobetko had his assignment in the south of Croatia, and so I don't know why this information -- because if I, as chief of the Main Staff, and other people who are mentioned don't feel the need to report this to General Bobetko, I don't know why this particular officer, holding that rank, took it upon himself to write to General Bobetko, and to write to me, or Stojic, or whoever else he was writing to, because he was not in the chain of command in Rama. He was just passing by, so it wasn't his job to do anything like that or write any reports at all. He was supposed to go to Bugojno, which was his place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now move on and deal with other members of the joint criminal enterprise, members who are alive. In the list, the first person mentioned is Mr. Prlic. Could you tell me when you met Mr. Prlic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I met him before this meeting was held on the 3rd of July, 1992, because up until then, to be quite frank, apart from Mr. Boban and apart from the people who were in Grude municipality, I did not meet any other officers who were in Herceg-Bosna. And as far as I know, the government there and the authorities there, as of the 3rd -- they were formed on the 3rd of September [as interpreted], after that date, and then they began functioning. So I never met Mr. Prlic before that. I think that he was -- whether he was in Mostar or somewhere else, I'm not quite sure, but -- the 3rd of July. So -- and perhaps August when he became president of the HVO, but not frequently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd just like to correct the transcript. In line 19, the word "officers" was used. The general spoke about officials, officials whom he had not met. So not "officers," but "officials." Yes, that's right now, "officials."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You say that you met Mr. Prlic on the 3rd of July, 1992, for the first time. When you met him, what was your impression of him, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I can joke about it, I thought it was my double, because we were sort of -- had the same haircuts. So people would say "Mr. Prlic," and "Mr. Petkovic," so I was very happy to see that there was somebody else who looked like me, who resembled me. But joking apart, I heard from others about Mr. Prlic first. And people said, as far as I knew, that he was the director, whether up until the war or before the war, the director of a large agricultural concern in the Neretva Valley, perhaps one of the largest in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that he was very successful in that job. Whether the company was called Apro Herzegovina or whatever, but, anyway, it was an agricultural concern. It had vineyards, fruit, processing plants, and so on and so forth. So that's what I had heard about him before I met him. And I think I also knew he was already working as a professor, whether at the university or at some other schools in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you must have met him on several occasions after the month of July 1992, I won't enter into any details. In the conversations that you had with Mr. Prlic, did he tell you that he was there to recreate the Banovina, that he was there for the Greater Croatia, that he was there to achieve Croatian majority, et cetera, et cetera? Did he tell you all those things in order to share with you this -- a common project, in a sense?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. In my first contact with Mr. Prlic, except for the introduction, saying who I was, where I came from, et cetera, we didn't discuss anything else. And I can tell you that I did not meet Mr. Prlic so frequently, because his position was such that he had a group of people he was working with, whereas I, until August or September, stayed in Grude, then I moved to Mostar, but even in Mostar we were not close to one another, except when there was a concrete invitation to attend a government meeting. Let me just tell you that the only time I sat down to have lunch with Mr. Prlic was the day when I was leaving Herceg-Bosna on the 5th of August, 1994. Never before that did we sit down to have a drink, or have lunch, or anything like that. So I didn't have conversations with various officials of Herceg-Bosna. And as far as I can remember, Mr. Prlic did not come frequently to Grude. Where he went after his working hours, was it Citluk, Makarska, I don't know where his parents or his family were living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said at a certain point that you didn't frequently meet with him, except when there were meetings of the government; page 30, line 12. Could you tell me, what were these government meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have seen documents that have been admitted into evidence here. Was it three times that I was invited to attend a government meeting to present the military situation in certain areas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me what, for you, the president of the HVO represented, the function that Mr. Prlic exercised? What was it, in fact, this position president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, or at least that was the interpretation, that it was a provisional executive body which was intended to assist lower-level bodies of authorities; that is, municipal organs of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us this is a provisional executive body. Those were the words you used. This provisional executive body --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- by what was it later replaced, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of July, or maybe the 27th of August - I don't want to guess - it became the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, when there were discussions about the union of republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a possible structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that the Republic of Herceg-Bosna came into existence on the 27th or 28th of July, 1993, which is not in the transcript, but I think that is the correct date. And in this Republic of Herceg-Bosna, what was the role of Mr. Prlic? Was it the same role that he played before, or had his role evolved, developed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same role. It was a provisional organ of authority in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, though it was at the time called the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall come back to my question once again. You are saying that the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was a temporary or provisional body. Could you tell me, by whom was this -- by what was this provisional body substituted?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I say "provisional body," we had to wait for the end of negotiations on the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan and the establishment of a union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the solution suggested by the international community, and I believe that all those who held certain positions at the time did so on a provisional basis. And once a signature had been placed on the document as a result of agreement of all parties, the situation would change. And until such a document was signed, in my view, all this was temporary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Here again we come to an extremely important question. When I put important questions, I issue a warning first. Could you tell me if Mr. Prlic, in his capacity as president of the HVO and later within the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, as a temporary organ, did Mr. Prlic give you orders of a military nature; that is, offensive action, defensive action, control of your acts and movements, from the military standpoint?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the government is no operative commander, and it does not issue commands. The government, at its meetings, discusses military issues, takes decisions, makes conclusions which later on, through the Defence Department and the Main Staff, may be transformed into certain orders. But the government is not an operative commander, but it does have the right to adopt decisions, conclusions, and recommendations at its meetings, even when matters of defensive -- of a defensive character are discussed. But it does not have the right to issue direct orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your reply is in the transcript, and you say that in your view, the government does not have the competence to issue orders of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I said that the government does not have the competence to issue military orders, but the government, when reviewing certain issues, may adopt conclusions, decisions, recommendations which, through the institutions such as the Defence Department, could reach the Main Staff or could be addressed for consideration by the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, you have told us last week that the military were under the control of the political authorities. Now, I wonder how this is to be reconciled, what you are telling us today; namely, that in a way the civil authorities had no authority over the military.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Trechsel, that is not what I said. I said that they could not issue operative orders. But within the framework of the executive authority, be it provisional or a government, there is a defence department, and through the Defence Department the civilian authorities do have influence, within certain limits, on the defence structure, that is, the army, the armed forces. On the other hand, at government meetings there were briefings about the situation on the battle-field, and the government would pass recommendations or conclusions or decisions as to what should be done. After all, the government received six-monthly reports on these activities, so this could be viewed as civilian supervision or monitoring of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, thanks to my colleague's question, I may perhaps refine a question further. If my understanding is correct, the government could make suggestions, or recommendations, or assessments of a situation, but the taking -- the final taking of a decision would fall upon either the headquarters or the supreme commander, either the Main Staff or the supreme commander, but under no circumstances would it be the government. Is that how we should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. When we are talking about direct operative commands, those are not done by the government. But if we are talking about recommendations, decisions, or conclusions, they can either go through the Defence Department to the Main Staff or such recommendations may, through a different channel, be addressed to the supreme commander. And we have seen several such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take a theoretical example, which does not relate to any particular situation, to understand properly what you're saying, because this is -- it is extremely difficult and complicated. Let us imagine, in a certain situation, that there is a government meeting. You're attending that meeting, and the Defence Department says, for instance, the following: In such and such a municipality, we have so many soldiers. We are in an inferior position in relation to the ABiH. It would be highly desirable to mobilise further, even to bring professional military units, even to re-subordinate certain brigades. That would be the best solution, from the logistic point of view, so as not to lose ground, militarily, and to safe-guard the interests of Herceg-Bosna. The Defence Department provides such an analysis and makes a proposition or a recommendation. Does this mean that in this case that I have just described, the final decision will be up to you, as chief of the Main Staff, or would it be up to Mr. Boban; that is, that you and Mr. Boban may be in agreement with the recommendation, but it is you who would decide, or maybe you are not in agreement, and in that event the decision may be a different one?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, in your question there are things that the chief of staff could do and also things that the supreme commander should do. For instance, if certain brigades needed to be pulled out from a certain territory, then such a request would be addressed to the supreme commander for him to decide that such and such a brigade should leave a certain terrain and move to another. However, if the decision would be to request additional mobilisation to reinforce the forces, then the Main Staff needs to establish the defences and to protect the interests of the Croats in that area. In one's work, one has to be very precise as to whom one should address. It's not possible to ask a question and leave it up to either the Main Staff or the supreme commander to decide. You have seen here in the proceedings that there was a request to move certain brigades, and this was addressed to the supreme commander. So some things that were reviewed were directly addressed to the supreme commander, and there were other things, other requests, that were addressed to the Main Staff for it to protect the Croatian territory in a certain area that was at risk, specifically, the situation in Konjic, or decisions of the 17th of April by the government to protect the Croatian areas, but also to engage in negotiations with the other side to deal with it by peaceful means. So these things had to be addressed either -- or proposed either to the supreme commander or the Main Staff, but not to leave it up to someone to choose who would be the one to make the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this theoretical example and your answer, I have to conclude that, in any event, it is either the supreme commander or the chief of staff who would decide, and never the government.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite. I said that the government proposes, and I have mentioned two specific examples from June 1993, addressed to the supreme commander, and another one from April that was addressed to the Main Staff, to strengthen the defences of certain Croatian areas, but also to engage in political discussions with the other party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we'll have the break now. I'll leave the subject of Mr. Prlic now, and after the break we'll address the subject of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. Mr. Stewart, there's something you'd like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. It's just this: that the Prosecution has responded to a motion from the accused Coric, or motions -- requests from the accused Coric and the accused Praljak. Their request, those co-accused, was to directly cross-examine Mr. Petkovic. The Prosecution response includes a request that if that application on behalf of Coric and Praljak is granted, they should have additional time, by reference to the guide-lines, to cross-examine Mr. Petkovic. Your Honours, we were not the people who -- we were not the Defence who filed the original motion or, of course, responded, but we would ask leave to reply on that particular point. Clearly, that affects us and the Petkovic Defence, but, in a sense, we've not yet participated in this particular exercise. So may we have leave, under 126 bis, to put in a reply dealing with that particular point in the Prosecution response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, I will hand down an oral decision. You will listen to it, and then you can see whether there are any other submissions you would like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber hereby hands down an oral decision on the requests made by the Coric and Praljak Defence teams, requests for the participation of the accused Valentin Coric and Slobodan Praljak in the cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic. It's a unanimous oral decision. The Coric and Praljak Defence have filed two requests on the participation of the accused Valentin Coric and Slobodan Praljak in the cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic. This was done on the 9th and 15th of February, 2010, respectively. On the 19th of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence and the Prosecution informed the parties that they did not object to the accused Valentin Coric and Slobodan Praljak participating in the cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic. In its response, the Prosecution, nevertheless, pointed out that it did not object to the requests, provided that the points dealt with by the accused Valentin Coric and Slobodan Praljak in the course of the cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic, were part of their specific expertise, in the sense of what was stated in the Appeal Chamber's decision of the 11th of September, 2008. The Trial Chamber would like to point out that the other parties did not file any responses to these two requests. The Chamber would like to point out that paragraph 3 of Guide-lines 1 of the decision of the 24th of April, 2008, authorises an accused, represented by counsel, to directly address a witness in the course of that witness's cross-examination in exceptional circumstances and provided that this has been authorised by the Chamber. The Chamber, in addition, stated in its guide-lines, as it had already done in its decision of the 10th of May, 2007, that exceptional circumstances are linked either to examining issues with regard to which the accused has specific knowledge or to the examination of issues that concern events that the person personally participated in. The Chamber notes that in its decision of the 11th of September, 2008, the Appeals Chamber pointed out that the assessment of the specific competence of an accused by the Chamber should be carried out on a case-by-case basis and should be done in a flexible manner. As a result, the Chamber hereby decides to authorise the accused Valentin Coric and Slobodan Praljak to participate in the cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic, provided that in the course of their cross-examination, the accused address the issue of events that they personally participated in or deal with certain matters for which they have specific competence. So this is our oral decision, which grants Mr. Praljak and Mr. Coric leave to put questions to General Petkovic at an appropriate time, but there are two conditions which have been set. First of all, the questions put must relate to specific competence that they may have to military issues, or it is necessary for Mr. Coric and Mr. Praljak to have participated in certain events, and in such a case they may put questions to General Petkovic. That is, therefore, our decision. Mr. Stewart, in the light of what has just been said, is there anything you would like to ask us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, thank you, I certainly see, with respect, the sense of hearing Your Honour's oral decision first in relation to that. The question which arises is whether it does -- whether it does leave alive the issue which we wished to address. One view is that since -- since Your Honours, in giving a ruling on this motion by the Coric and the Praljak Defenses, and therefore, by the same token, on the Prosecution response, have not actually said anything about the Prosecution request for additional time, that implicitly, Your Honours, have not granted that request. If that's correct, if Your Honours have, in effect, implicitly rejected the Prosecution request in its response for additional time, then I'll just sit down because there's nothing to reply to. But if that remains a live issue and is not yet firmly resolved, then I do ask for leave to reply and deal specifically with that point. So I just need some clarification as to where we stand. Well, Mr. Scott is literally standing, so he can tell me where he metaphorically stands as well, and then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. I think there's not a major issue here. The Prosecution's position was, I think, that to the extent that the request otherwise satisfy the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and the rulings this Chamber in terms of allowing an accused to conduct cross-examine personally, we said as long as it meets the usual rules, we have no further objection beyond that. Secondly, we said that to the extent that on cross-examination new topics were raised, again keeping with the regular rules that if a new topic is raised, that it becomes direct examination, that direct examination has to time -- has to be charged against some sort of bank of available time, and no leading questions will be asked. In the usual rule, no special favours, no special privileges being asked by the Prosecution. But if that's the case and if there is additional direct examination under those rules, then the Prosecution gets the equivalent amount of time to cross on that -- on those points. Those are the rules of the Chamber for a long time. That's all we said, was, depending on what happens, we, of course, reserve the opportunity to request that the normal rules apply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that does leave an issue. It's a narrow issue; it's not unimportant. But the issues of no leading questions and time counting against the bank of time for other accused, those don't concern us. We're not squabbling about those. And to a considerable extent, they're clear under the guide-lines. But the very last issue, and it's the only point on which we wanted leave to reply, it's the only live point as far as we're concerned, is the very last thing Mr. Scott said; that then he wants to have additional time. That's additional to what is the standard allocation under the guide-lines, additional time equivalent to the time spent by Mr. Coric or Mr. Praljak personally in cross-examining on topics which have not been raised on direct examination by Ms. Alaburic in examining Mr. Petkovic. So it's that single live issue, but it does apparently remain live. And we have not yet -- without leave to reply, we have had no opportunity to deal with that -- we would have had no opportunity to deal with a point which does directly affect us. So that's the basis of my application, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber will meet tomorrow afternoon, and we will respond to what you have said, and we will also respond to what the Prosecution has submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To what I've said, Your Honour, or to what we would file by way of reply on the basis of the leave that I'm requesting? That's -- is Your Honour giving -- our reply is -- well, for practical purposes -- Ms. Alaburic will want to have a look at it. It's for practical purposes going to be ready to file. So is Your Honour -- are Your Honours giving me leave and then inviting me to file that pretty much straight away so that Your Honours will be able to consider everything in time to rule tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, file your submissions, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, we will now continue and talk about Mr. Bruno Stojic. We know that you met him. You returned by car with him on the 9th of May. But we'll start from the beginning again. On which day, exactly, did you meet Mr. Stojic for the first time in your life?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first time I met Mr. Stojic was on the 14th of April, 1992, when I arrived in Grude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So prior to the 14th of April, 1992, you had never seen him. As in the case of Mr. Prlic, my question is: What impression did you have of him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. So that means he didn't leave an impression of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you are referring to now. Prlic or to Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To Mr. Stojic. When you met Mr. Stojic, what was your impression of him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's impossible to decide what one's impression is at the first meeting. From the 15th of April, 1992, Mr. Stojic and I worked together in the separate composition of the forward command post, but Mr. Stojic was responsible for the logistics needs within that forward command post. And that's what we did until the 3rd of July, 1992, which is when Mr. Stojic was appointed by Mr. Boban to the position of the head of the Defence Department. As far as his duties are concerned, at the time he performed his duties very well and to the extent that it was possible, logistically, for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say from the 14th of April, 1992, until the 13th of July, 1992, so for about three months, you had contact with Mr. Stojic because he dealt with logistic matters. When you would meet, did Mr. Stojic express his personal political views, did he speak to you about the Banovina, Greater Croatia, about a Croatian majority that should be established, about the expulsion of Muslims, and so on and so forth? Did he address all these matters, or did you talk about other things?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, he didn't address such subjects because there were other issues at the time that had to be urgently dealt with, and I never spoke to Mr. Stojic or to anyone else about the issues that you have just listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stojic became the head of the Defence Department in July 1992. In that capacity, at the end of 1992 and in the course of 1993, and in 1994 too, would he tell you, I have in mind, the desire to see once more a Croatian banovina, a Greater Croatia, and so on and so forth? Did he talk to you about such things or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another important question for you. Please listen carefully. It's a new warning. As head of the Defence Department and then as minister of defence of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, did Mr. Stojic give you orders, instructions, relating to ongoing military operations or relating to military operations that should be undertaken?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Stojic, first of all, had to establish the Defence Department as a body of the temporary executive authorities, and together with that body, and they're responsible for the defence of the Croats and areas inhabited by Croats and other peoples. So that was the first task to be dealt with. Mr. Stojic was at the head of a professional body which was part of the executive authorities, and he was a link between those authorities and the Main Staff, or, rather, the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Mr. Stojic, in the course of his work, had recourse to orders, decisions, solutions. It depended on the situation that had to be dealt with. He would deal with problems that were legally his responsibility, his responsibility pursuant to decrees. Other decisions were matters that came under the administrative part of his work. Mr. Bruno Stojic did not issue an operative order to commence with operations of any kind in the territory of the HZ-HB. Such operations, apart from in 1992 -- well, there were no such operations in the territory of the HZ-HB, apart from in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have just said that Mr. Stojic did not issue orders of an operational nature. Let me take an example. Let us imagine that for an Operation X, you informed the minister of defence that you need five tanks, artillery pieces, tonnes of food, so many doctors, and you ask him that he take the necessary steps. Let us imagine that he says to you, It is out of the question, General Petkovic, to engage in such a military operation, because I, as the defence minister, believe that it should not take place for such and such a reason. Therefore, I will not allow it. Is that possible or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible, because he was the head of the Defence Department, and so if he found that an operation -- well, we're speaking in principle, of course. He could have put a stop to any operation of this kind if it was not considered to be in the interests of the defence of the territory on which the Croats were living, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he did have the ability to prohibit an operation if, at his level, he felt that the interests of the defence of the territory did not require such an operation. So you're telling me this. Did this happen at all, or did it never happen?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, something like that never happened. Mr. Stojic would brief the authorities about a situation, and if tanks were mentioned and so on, and if need be, he would make the requests that the army needed. He would ask the authorities, whether it be weapons, or financial resources, or other materiel, or material resources, or whatever. So he also had to consult the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this brings me to General Praljak. When did you meet General Praljak for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was on the 19th of April, 1992, when I went to Citluk and visited him there. He was the commander of the Operative Group of South-East Herzegovina, I believe, at the time. So it was the fifth day -- the fourth or fifth day after my arrival in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was commander of the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina of the HVO or the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the 19th of April, 1992, you heard General Praljak mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I hope General Praljak won't mind -- won't be angry with me if I say that I didn't hear anything about General Praljak at all, because he was in quite another part of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the same question as for the others. When you met him for the first time, what was the impression he gave you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I met a man who was very eloquent when speaking. He was very demanding towards those whom he commanded. He didn't like talking about certain matters much, and he had his very own way of going about things; issuing orders, dispatching people, giving advice, counselling, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
